player_0.content: New plan: I correctly formalized the premises and deduced that the specific individual $a$ (who is a sister of Ruth but not a schoolmate of Karen) must be a classmate of Marisa. However, I failed to recognize that this deduction ($R(a) \land C(a)$) directly contradicts the conclusion ($\exists x (R(x) \land \neg C(x))$). Since the premises force the existence of a sister of Ruth who *is* a classmate of Marisa, and do not guarantee the existence of one who is *not*, the argument is invalid. My mistake was stopping the analysis before explicitly comparing the derived fact ($C(a)$) with the required conclusion ($\neg C(x)$). Next time, after deriving the properties of the existential instance from the premises, I will explicitly check if those properties satisfy the conclusion. If the premises force a condition that contradicts the conclusion (or fail to support it), I will immediately classify the argument as "invalid" and provide the final answer.
